title: India Faces Rising Dengue Threat as Monsoon Fuels Mosquito Breeding Across Cities
excerpt: Delhi reports 348 dengue cases with hospitals seeing 8-10 daily admissions, while Mumbai and NCR cities also witness surging vector-borne disease numbers amid heavy monsoon rains.
body:
• Delhi has recorded 348 dengue cases through early August 2026, with hospitals reporting severe infections involving liver dysfunction and capillary leak.
  • Dengue cases spiked to 277 by end of July in Delhi-NCR — among the highest mid-year tallies in five years — while malaria cases reached 124, already exceeding last year's full-year count.
  • Mosquito larvae breeding has been found at 2.40 lakh sites across Delhi this year, prompting MCD to issue notices to 1.29 lakh homes.
  • Mumbai's BMC has issued a health alert following a surge in dengue, malaria, and leptospirosis cases linked to waterlogging and stagnant water from continuous rainfall.

Delhi Hospitals Under Pressure

Several major hospitals across Delhi are witnessing a sharp rise in dengue admissions as the monsoon season intensifies. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi's latest available report, released on August 7, recorded 348 dengue cases through August 5 — a number health officials acknowledge likely understates the true scale of infections.

"We are seeing dengue patient admissions. Those with severe infection are suffering from liver dysfunction and capillary leak."

— Dr. Sumit Ray, Medical Director, Holy Family Hospital, Delhi

A senior doctor at a South Delhi hospital reported 8-10 daily dengue admissions, calling it a "fairly high number." Fortis Hospital alone recorded 15 dengue cases from August 1 onward. The MCD has notably stopped releasing its regular weekly vector-borne disease reports, even as a senior civic official claimed the "situation is under control."

Breeding Sites Spread Across the Capital

The scale of mosquito breeding across Delhi paints a concerning picture. Civic authorities have examined 2.85 crore locations for mosquito larvae this year, finding breeding activity at 2.40 lakh sites — more than double the 1.13 lakh sites recorded in the same period in 2022. The MCD has issued notices to owners of 1.29 lakh houses and levied penalties at more than 56,000 locations.

Delhi's weather conditions are creating ideal breeding environments, with average temperatures around 30°C and 78% humidity, combined with approximately 206 mm of rainfall over the past fortnight. The Aedes and Anopheles mosquitoes that transmit dengue and malaria multiply fastest near 29°C in standing water that accumulates after rain.

NCR and Mumbai Also Affected

The threat extends well beyond Delhi's borders. Dr. Rajesh Kumar Budhiraja, Director of Internal Medicine at Fortis Faridabad, reported that dengue cases spiked to 277 by end of July across Delhi-NCR — among the highest mid-year tallies in the past five years. Malaria cases had reached 124 by late July, already exceeding the previous year's record.

In Mumbai, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation issued a health alert following continuous monsoon rains that have caused widespread waterlogging. The BMC reported a surge in dengue, malaria, and leptospirosis cases. More than 350 malaria cases were reported in Mumbai in July alone, according to BMC data.

Health Advisory and Prevention

Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh reviewed the city's dengue preparedness, noting that the government has strengthened surveillance across 35 sentinel surveillance hospitals, activated real-time case reporting through the Integrated Health Information Platform, and established a control room at the Directorate General of Health Services to coordinate response efforts.

Health experts are urging the public to take precautions including eliminating stagnant water in and around homes, using mosquito repellents containing DEET or Picaridin, installing window screens, wearing protective clothing, and seeking immediate medical attention for symptoms like high fever, severe headache, joint pain, or rash.

"The fight against dengue cannot be won by government efforts alone. Every citizen must ensure that mosquito breeding does not take place in and around their homes."

— Pankaj Kumar Singh, Delhi Health Minister

What Travelers Should Know

With August and September typically being peak months for dengue transmission in India, travelers planning visits to Delhi, Mumbai, and other Indian cities during the monsoon season should take extra precautions. The WHO recommends using mosquito nets, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and applying insect repellent regularly. Anyone experiencing high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, or muscle and joint pain after visiting affected areas should seek medical evaluation promptly.
